readerTitle: Two friends start a bakery: what to agree before the first loaf
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집, B2B 마케팅 에이전시) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 친구끼리 하는 창업일수록 지분은 시간에 걸쳐 얻게 하고, 누가 무엇을 최종 결정하는지는 사이가 좋을 때 미리 정해 둔다.
misconception: 친한 친구라면 50:50으로 나누고 모든 일을 함께 정하면 공평하고 충분하다.

sources.text: 창업자 지분 베스팅과 의사결정 권한 배분에 관한 일반적인 창업 실무 개념
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 베스팅 계산: 4년(48개월) 베스팅, 1년 클리프, 이후 매월 균등 베스팅 가정. 18개월 시점 Maya의 확보 지분 = 50% × 18 ÷ 48 = 18.75%. 미확보 지분 = 50% − 18.75% = 31.25%.
"4년 베스팅, 1년 클리프가 스타트업에서 흔하다"는 일반적인 실무 관행으로 서술했습니다. 특정 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
국가별 법률·세무 조언은 범위 밖입니다. 7번 카드에서 '나라마다 규칙이 다르니 현지 전문가와 문서화하라'는 일반적인 안내만 했습니다.

cards.title: Two friends start a bakery
body: Jo is a gifted baker. Maya is great with numbers. They've been friends since school, and they each put in the same savings to open a small bakery.
Their whole agreement is a handshake: "50/50, we decide everything together." It feels fair. It also leaves two big questions unanswered.

image.label: Two friends shaking hands in front of an empty bakery
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 아직 간판이 없는 작은 빵집 앞에서 두 친구가 악수. 한 명은 앞치마, 다른 한 명은 노트북을 들고 있음. 진열대는 비어 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should they hold their shares?
body: Jo will bake full time. Maya will run the books and suppliers, and quit her office job once the bakery is stable. Both expect to stay for years.
Which ownership setup protects them best?

options.text: 50/50 from day one. They trust each other.
options.feedback: Simple and friendly. But if one of them leaves early, they keep half the bakery the other one goes on building. Trust doesn't cover a change of plans.

options.text: 50/50, but each earns their half over four years of working in the bakery
options.feedback: This is **vesting**: ownership is earned over time. It stays fair even if life changes for one of them.

options.text: Split by hours worked each month, recalculated as they go
options.feedback: It rewards effort, but recounting ownership every month invites constant arguments. Vesting gets the fairness with one rule set once.

cards.title: Maya gets an offer she can't refuse.
body: Her old employer offers her a big promotion. She steps away from the bakery, and Jo carries on alone. Here is what Maya owns under each setup, assuming four-year vesting with a one-year *cliff* (nothing is earned before month 12).

breakdown.label: No vesting
breakdown.detail: Maya keeps half, though Jo will do all the work from now on

breakdown.label: Returned
breakdown.detail: Unearned shares go back, ready for whoever replaces Maya

cards.callout: Vesting doesn't punish Maya. It matches ownership to the time she actually gave.

cards.title: "We decide everything together" stops working.
body: Back to month 6, before Maya left. Jo wants a new sourdough line. Maya wants to raise croissant prices first. Each waits for the other to agree.
With a 50/50 split and no rules, every disagreement is a tie. Small choices sit for weeks. Jo starts quietly changing recipes without asking, and Maya notices.

cards.title: How should they make decisions?
body: They agree they need a better way. Which works best?

options.text: Keep deciding everything together, just talk more
options.feedback: More talking feels kind, but two equal votes still deadlock. Busy owners end up acting alone, which breaks trust faster.

options.text: Each gets final say in their own area, and a short list of big decisions needs both
options.feedback: Clear **roles and decision rights** let daily choices move fast while protecting the choices that could sink the business.

options.text: Jo works more hours, so Jo has the final say on everything
options.feedback: Decisions get faster, but Maya loses any say over the money she's responsible for. Final say should follow the area, not the hours.

cards.title: One page, signed while they still got along.
body: They put it on a single page:
list: **Jo decides:** menu, recipes, kitchen staff schedule
**Maya decides:** prices, supplier contracts, the books
**Both must agree:** hiring, borrowing money, a second shop, selling the business
**If they're stuck:** a trusted mentor they both chose breaks the tie
cards.callout: The sourdough launched in two weeks. The price rise went live a week later.
cards.softwareNote: In software startups, four-year vesting with a one-year cliff is a common default, and split areas often look like product versus sales. The same page works for an app as for a bakery.

cards.title: Paper can't fix a mismatch in commitment.
body: Vesting and decision rights make change fair. They don't make a reluctant partner committed. If one friend never planned to stay, have that talk first.
Cash is different from work, too. If one founder puts in much more money, that may need its own terms instead of being folded into the same vesting.
Rules on ownership differ by country. Write it down with a local professional.

image.label: A signed one-page agreement pinned on a bakery wall
image.brief: 빵집 주방 벽 코르크보드에 한 장짜리 합의서가 꽂혀 있고, 두 개의 서명. 옆에 밀가루 자국과 레시피 메모. 글씨는 읽히지 않게 흐릿하게. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's a marketing agency.
body: Two former colleagues start an agency for local businesses. Sam wins clients. Lee runs the projects and the freelancers. They want to split 50/50.

options.text: 50/50 now, and they decide every deal and hire together
options.feedback: Equal and open, but no **vesting** if one leaves, and every proposal waits on two people. Clients don't wait.

options.text: 50/50 earned over four years; Sam owns pricing and deals, Lee owns delivery and freelancers; contracts above a set size need both
options.feedback: **Vesting** keeps ownership fair over time, and clear **decision rights** let each move fast while big bets stay shared.

options.text: 50/50 earned over four years, but Sam decides everything since clients pay the bills
options.feedback: The vesting is right. But Sam could promise work Lee can't deliver, and Lee has no say. Split final say by area.

cards.title: Agree how ownership is earned and who decides what, before the first sale.
body: This lesson used two ideas: **vesting**, so ownership follows the time each founder gives, and **roles and decision rights**, so daily choices move fast and big ones stay shared.
**Try it today:** write down three decisions in your business and who has the final say on each. If the answer is "we'll see," decide now.
